before:
So set one boundary. "What's a 'boundary'?", I might be asking. That looks like saying no to something that's costing you too much (money, time, whatever it is). Throw the moldy bread in the trash. Handle that task you've been putting off, or the tax man, or your DUIs in Maryland, even if all you do today is open the envelope. Keep one small promise to your little one. Clean your room! And if a relationship keeps making you less safe, leave it, which is not a small thing at all, I know. Your little one has had enough grown-ups who said sweet things and then did nothing, so this is how they start to believe you.

You can protect your little one from yourself too, like by repairing after an internal attack. "What's an 'internal attack'?" Calling yourself an idiot for losing your keys again, for one. Your little one was listening, so you go back and apologize to them. If they're sarcastic about it, you let it go by instead of snapping back. They don't trust you yet, and you don't ask them to. They complain about something, they're right, and you say so. All of that shows as clearly to them as the clean room did. It's proof you love them, but they can still tell the difference between being put up with and being loved.
after: (Not written yet. The next paragraph will be about picking one of these acts and making it specific: when, the smallest first step, what help it needs, a short rehearsal for a hard moment you can see coming, and looking afterward at what actually happened. Leave all of that to it.)
brief:
- When you can't find much warmth for your little one yet (the Nurturer isn't showing up), the Protector can be the one who starts the relationship.
- At first, care may look like the guide's own examples: a meal, a cancelled obligation, a locked door, or the phone put down at midnight. Earlier the article already had "lock the door and get help" and "If you're about to send an angry text, hit pause", so lean on the other examples or call back to those; don't pile on new invented scenes.
- Warmth can come later.
Note: the paragraph before ends on "they can still tell the difference between being put up with and being loved." This paragraph can react to that: what if love isn't there yet? Don't contradict the article's stance that love matters and doesn't have to wait for trust (the next section says so); this is about where you can start, not about love being unnecessary. "The Nurturer" and "the Protector" are already introduced in the article, as two of the three jobs one grown-up does (the third is the Guide).
Your first sentence will be read together with the last lines of the paragraph before. There, openers that start a new topic ("Then there's…", "Some of it happens…") or keep a run of commands going have failed.
Limits: don't invent facts about the author's life, and don't write "I" for him; never call the inner child "the kid"; don't reuse the paragraphs before's items (the boundary, moldy bread, tax man, clean room, keys, sarcasm).
